content: 1. B. Obie Baizley, DC: A chiropractor from Manitoba, Canada, who also served as a politician. 2. Fred Barge, DC: An influential author who wrote extensively on chiropractic topics, ranging from philosophy to practice management. He was elected President of the International Chiropractor's Association in 1988 and was a historian who contributed numerous articles on chiropractic and its practitioners. He also founded the journal Chiropractic History. 3. Henri Gillet, DC: A Belgian chiropractor who developed the Motion Palpation technique in response to the Belgian government prohibiting chiropractors from taking X-rays. 4. Clarence Gonstead, DC: The developer of the Gonstead technique and founder of the Mt. Horeb Clinic. 5. George Goodheart, DC: The creator of Applied Kinesiology and the first chiropractor to serve the U.S. Olympic Team. 6. Gerry E. Hinton, DC: A chiropractor who also served as a Louisiana State Senator. 7. Earl Homewood, DC: The President of the Canadian Memorial Chiropractic College (CMCC) and author of Neurodynamics of Vertebral Subluxation. 8. Fred Illi, DC: A Swiss chiropractor and a pioneering researcher in chiropractic during the first half of the 20th century. He developed theories on the role of spinal biomechanics in the human body and collaborated with Joseph Janse at the National College in Chicago. 9. Teddy Infuhr, DC: A former child actor who became a chiropractor. 10. William Ivens, DC: A chiropractor who served as a member of the Manitoba Legislature in Canada. 11. Joseph Janse, DC: A key figure in chiropractic education, he helped establish the independently chartered Council on Chiropractic Education (CCE). As President of the National College (now National University of Health Sciences), he led the institution to become the first chiropractic college to achieve federally recognized status. He was also a renowned anatomist and founded the Journal of Manipulative and Physiological Therapeutics. 12. Bernard Jensen, DC: The inventor of the controversial practice of Iridology. 13. Joseph C. Keating, PhD: A clinical psychologist who dedicated his career to teaching and researching chiropractic. He is best known for his published works as a historian of chiropractic. 14. Hugh Logan, DC: The founder of the Logan Basic Technique, which is based on the theory that continuous pressure on a pelvic ligament with deep sensory reflex adjusts a spinal segment. He also founded and served as the first president of Logan College of Chiropractic. 15. D.D. Palmer (Daniel David Palmer), DC: The founder of modern chiropractic in the late 19th century. He theorized that the body has a natural healing power mediated by the nervous system. He believed that spinal misalignments, or vertebral subluxations, could disrupt nervous input to organs, leading to dysfunction. His first chiropractic adjustments in 1895 reportedly restored hearing to one man and alleviated heart trouble in another. He later established the Palmer Infirmary and Cure in 1897, which evolved into the Palmer School of Chiropractic. 16. B.J. Palmer (Bartlett Joshua Palmer), DC: The son of D.D. Palmer, he took over the Palmer School of Chiropractic in 1904 and significantly advanced the profession. His contributions included research, improved spinal adjustment techniques, higher educational standards, and global recognition of chiropractic. He also overcame legal and financial challenges to secure licensing for chiropractors. Despite controversies, by the time of his death in 1961, chiropractic had become firmly established as a health science. 17. David D. Palmer, DC: The grandson of D.D. Palmer, he became President of Palmer School in 1961. He modernized the campus, introduced teaching aids, and changed the institution's name to Palmer College of Chiropractic as part of efforts toward accreditation. He also established a non-profit status for the college and organized the Palmer College of Chiropractic International Alumni Association. After his death in 1978, the college achieved accreditation from the Council on Chiropractic Education and the North Central Association of Colleges and Schools. 18. Mabel Palmer, DC: The wife of B.J. Palmer, she became a chiropractor in 1905 and was a recognized authority on anatomy. She taught at the Palmer School for over 30 years and was a close advisor to her husband in all aspects of the chiropractic profession. 19. Jim Parker, DC: The founder of Parker College of Chiropractic in Texas. 20. John Lyle Robinson, DC: A chiropractor who served as a member of the Canadian Parliament. 21. Walter Wardwell, PhD: A sociologist and historian known for his lifelong interest and research in chiropractic. He authored the definitive history of the profession, Chiropractic: History and Evolution of a New Profession, as well as numerous articles, including Social Factors in the Survival of Chiropractic: A Comparative View. He also wrote about the future direction of the chiropractic profession. 22. Clarence Weiant, DC, PhD: The first chiropractor to also hold a PhD (in anthropology). He worked at the Chiropractic Institute of New York (CINY) and published scientifically valid research promoting chiropractic, making him one of the profession's most important and eloquent spokespeople. 23. John Wolfe, DC: A graduate of Palmer College of Chiropractic, he founded Northwestern Health Sciences University on June 2, 1941. This institution includes a chiropractic college with an intensive focus on basic sciences. He served as the university's president for over 40 years.
